name: Dombra (Kazakh Two-String Lute)
description: Pear-shaped, long-necked two-stringed plucked lute of the Kazakh steppe, the country's signature instrument. Solo instrumental pieces (kuy) performed on dombra are central to Kazakh identity and the tradition of Dombra Kuy is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List. Legendary kuishi like Qurmangazy composed famous kuys on it, and epic singers accompanied their tales with the instrument.
material: wood (often apricot or pine), gut/nylon strings
era: ancient; kuy tradition documented from 19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Kazakh traditional art of Dombra Kuy' (2014); Kazakh National Museum

name: Qobyz (Kazakh Horsehair Fiddle)
description: Bowed two-string fiddle of shamans and bakhsy among the Kazakhs, carved from a single piece of wood with horsehair strings and a leather-covered resonator. Legend names Korkyt Ata as its inventor; its sound was held to drive away evil spirits, sickness and death. The qobyz remains the emblematic instrument of Kazakh epic and ritual tradition.
material: single block of wood (often apricot), horsehair strings, leather soundboard
source: Korkyt legends of the Book of Dede Korkut cycle; Qazaqstan heritage portal 'Kobyz and Korkut'; ar.culture.ru collections

name: Shanyrak (Yurt Crown)
description: The crown of the Kazakh yurt: a circular wooden rim with radiating cross-beams (uyk) that supports the roof and lets smoke and daylight pass through the top opening. Beyond architecture, the shanyrak is the foremost Kazakh symbol of home, family continuity and the nation; it stands at the centre of Kazakhstan's state emblem, and custom passes the family shanyrak to the household heir.
source: Akorda — National Emblem of Kazakhstan; ar.culture.ru 'Yurt'

name: Saukele (Kazakh Bridal Headdress)
description: Tall conical wedding headdress of Kazakh brides, covered with silver plaques, coral, beads and gemstones, with a fur-trimmed brow and long veils. The most expensive item of a bride's dowry after the yurt, the saukele symbolised the beginning of married life; it was handed down from mother to daughter and worn until the birth of the first child.
material: velvet or cloth, silver plaques, coral, beads, gold thread, fur
source: Omsk Museum of History and Regional Studies; ar.culture.ru 'Saukele'

name: Kamcha (Kazakh Whip)
description: Braided leather whip of the Kazakhs, carried by horsemen and elders as a riding tool and badge of authority. In Kazakh folklore the kamcha carried protective power: the whip of a respected man was hung near a woman in childbirth, and its crack was said to drive off evil spirits. Skilled craftsmen braid the lash from several plaited leather cords.
material: braided leather, wood or bone handle
source: e-history.kz 'The role of the horse in Kazakh culture' (2016); Kazinform feature on whip-braiding
